claim: Brain imaging can be used to study how individuals' brains are aging, compared against population norms.
source: Brain imaging can be used to study how individuals' brains are aging, compared against population norms.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the general application of brain imaging in aging research, supported by the methodology and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Smoking and blood pressure can be seen to accelerate brain aging.
source: This can inform on aspects of brain health; for example, smoking and blood pressure can be seen to accelerate brain aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the associations found between specific modes and these lifestyle/health factors as detailed in the Results section.

claim: 62 modes of subject variability were identified from 21,407 subjects' multimodal brain imaging data in UK Biobank.
source: here we identified 62 modes of subject variability, from 21,407 subjects' multimodal brain imaging data in UK Biobank.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the primary methodological outcome, with specific numbers of modes and subjects.

claim: The modes represent different aspects of brain aging, showing distinct patterns of functional and structural brain change.
source: The modes represent different aspects of brain aging, showing distinct patterns of functional and structural brain change, and distinct patterns of association with genetics, lifestyle, cognition, physical measures and disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed analysis of each mode's associations with different imaging modalities and non-imaging variables presented in the Results section.

claim: 34 modes had genetic associations while conventional brain-age modelling found no genetic associations.
source: While conventional brain-age modelling found no genetic associations, 34 modes had genetic associations.
evidence: This is directly supported by the GWAS results presented in Table 1 and Figure 3, showing 34 modes with replicated genetic associations at the higher threshold.

claim: It is important not to treat brain aging as a single homogeneous process.
source: We suggest that it is important not to treat brain aging as a single homogeneous process, and that modelling of distinct patterns of structural and functional change will reveal more biologically meaningful markers of brain aging in health and disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings that multiple distinct modes show different biological associations, supported by the comparative analysis with all-in-one models.

claim: Alzheimer's disease shows similar patterns of change to that of accelerated healthy aging.
source: For example, looking at structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, a high degree of atrophy would cause a subject's brain to appear older than a normal age-matched brain. Estimation of brain age and the delta is of value in studying both normal aging and disease, with some diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, showing similar patterns of change to that of accelerated healthy aging (Franke et al., 2010; Cole and Franke, 2017a; Cole et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The typical brain age prediction approach uses one or more imaging modalities, most commonly using just a single structural image from each subject.
source: The typical approach uses one or more imaging modalities, most commonly using just a single structural image from each subject.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, based on established knowledge of brain age prediction methods.

claim: Multiple distinct biological processes contribute to the changes seen in the brain with aging.
source: Hence, while the explicit goal of much brain-age research is to obtain a single estimate of brain age (and brain-age delta) per subject, one could nevertheless expect that multiple distinct biological processes contribute to the changes seen in the brain with aging.
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on biological reasoning, which is then tested and supported by the study's findings.

claim: Different biological factors affecting brain aging could have different age dependence with distinct population-averaged aging curves.
source: Further, different factors affecting brain aging could well have different age dependence - population-averaged aging curves for the different factors could be quite distinct (e.g. with respect to strength and linearity of the age dependence) (Kessler et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2018; Vinke et al., 2018; Douaud et al., 2014; Groves et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is demonstrated by the varying age curves shown in Figure 1.

claim: Different biological factors of brain aging might be expected to show distinct genetic influence.
source: Different biological factors of brain aging might well also be expected to show distinct genetic influence.
evidence: This is a logical expectation that is subsequently validated by the GWAS results showing different genetic associations for different modes.

claim: Six brain imaging modalities from UK Biobank were used to identify 62 distinct modes of population variation.
source: Here, we used six brain imaging modalities from UK Biobank (Miller et al., 2016) to identify 62 distinct modes of population variation, almost all of which showed significant age effects.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodology with citation to the UK Biobank imaging protocol.

claim: Almost all of the 62 modes showed significant age effects.
source: Here, we used six brain imaging modalities from UK Biobank (Miller et al., 2016) to identify 62 distinct modes of population variation, almost all of which showed significant age effects.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis showing 59 of 62 modes correlate significantly with age at the Bonferroni-corrected level.

claim: The multimodal brain imaging data came from 21,407 participants over the age of 45 years in UK Biobank.
source: We used the multimodal brain imaging data from 21,407 participants, over the age of 45y, in UK Biobank.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample characteristics.

claim: 3913 imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) were used in the analysis.
source: For this work we used 3913 IDPs (imaging-derived phenotypes, generated by our team on behalf of UK Biobank, and made available to all researchers by UK Biobank).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data used in the analysis.

claim: IDPs include functional and structural connectivity between specific pairs of regions, localised tissue microstructure and biological makeup, and the geometry of cortical and subcortical structures.
source: IDPs include functional and structural connectivity between specific pairs of regions, localised tissue microstructure and biological makeup, and the geometry of cortical and subcortical structures.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the types of measures included in the IDPs.

claim: Each mode is described by two vectors: a set of IDP weights and a set of subject weights.
source: Each mode is described by two vectors. The first is a set of IDP weights, describing which specific aspects of brain structure and function (i.e. which IDPs) are involved in that mode (e.g. a given mode might reflect volume of grey matter across various regions involved in language processing). The second is a set of subject weights (one value per subject), describing where in the population distribution a subject lies, in terms of strongly expressing a given mode of variation (e.g. a given subject might have considerably less grey matter in language regions than the population average).
evidence: This is a description of the ICA output structure.

claim: Virtually all modes show a significant aging effect.
source: These subject-weight vectors (one vector per mode) can be used to help understand the biological meaning of, and causal factors behind, the modes of population variation, by computing associations with non-imaging factors and genetics (a genetic or early-life factor that correlates, across subjects, with our hypothetical mode might suggest biological causes of changes in grey matter volume in the language network). Here we use the subject-weight vectors to study brain aging; virtually all modes show a significant aging effect (Figure 1), and in this work, we study the different aspects of brain aging represented by the 62 modes (as well as 6 clusters of these modes).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1 showing the aging curves and the statistical results indicating 59 of 62 modes are significantly age-correlated.

claim: After discarding outlier data and subjects with high levels of missing/outlier imaging data, 18,707 subjects were retained.
source: After discarding outlier data and subjects with high levels of missing/outlier imaging data, we retained data from 18,707 subjects (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data quality control procedure and resulting sample size.

claim: The mean absolute delta (error between age and predicted age) using all 62 modes together was 2.9 years.
source: Using all 62 modes together in an 'all-in-one' prediction of overall brain aging, mean absolute delta (the 'error' between age and predicted age) was 2.9y.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the prediction accuracy for the all-in-one model.

claim: Quantitative optimisation of the clustering dimensionality resulted in a meaningful reduction to six mode-clusters.
source: In order to help generate more parsimonious descriptions of the 62 modes of brain aging, we investigated whether clustering modes together into a smaller number of mode-clusters could provide a meaningful simplification. Quantitative optimisation of the clustering dimensionality resulted in a meaningful reduction to six mode-clusters (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clustering analysis outcome, with reference to the methods and supplementary figure.

claim: In most cases, individual modes are largely driven by IDPs from a single imaging modality.
source: In most cases, individual modes are largely driven by IDPs from a single imaging modality, with a few exceptions such as mode 5262.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of mode compositions shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mode-clusters mix more across modalities than individual modes.
source: Naturally, the mode-clusters mix more across modalities.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of clustering modes together and is observable in Figure 2.

claim: Separate GWAS were carried out for the brain-aging delta from each of the 62 modes and from the 6 mode-clusters.
source: We carried out a separate GWAS for the brain-aging delta from each of the 62 modes, and from the 6 mode-clusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the genetic analysis methodology.

claim: GWAS used 9,812,242 SNPs that passed all quality control tests.
source: GWAS used 9,812,242 SNPs (single-nucleotide polymorphisms) that passed all quality control tests (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the genetic data used in the analysis.

claim: 68 genetic associations from the 62 modes passed the more stringent Bonferroni-adjusted threshold.
source: 68 of these associations passed the more stringent threshold of 9.33, which increases the standard threshold by a Bonferroni factor of 62+6 to account for the multiple phenotypes' testing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the GWAS results at the higher threshold.

claim: 34 of the 62 modes have at least one significant genetic association at the higher threshold that replicates.
source: Of the 62 modes, 34 have at least one significant association at the higher threshold, and all these 34 modes have at least one association in the replication sample.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of modes with replicated genetic associations.

claim: From the 6 mode-clusters, 14 regions of the genome have significant associations at the higher threshold, 12 of which replicate.
source: From the 6 mode-clusters, 14 regions of the genome have significant associations at the higher threshold, 12 of which replicate.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the GWAS results for mode-clusters.

claim: Three of the 6 mode-clusters have at least one significant genetic association, including in replication.
source: Three of the these 6 mode-clusters have at least one significant association, including in replication.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of mode-clusters with replicated genetic associations.

claim: Two all-in-one brain-age delta estimations showed no genetic associations that were significant and replicated.
source: We also evaluated genetic associations for two 'all-in-one' estimations of a single best estimate of brain-age (and associated delta); we used all IDPs in one case, and all modes in the other. This was done with the methods described in Smith et al. (2019). These two all-in-one brain-age delta estimations showed no genetic assocations that were significant and replicated, consistent with previous GWAS of all-in-one brain-aging modelling (Ning et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the GWAS results for all-in-one models, with citation to previous consistent findings.

claim: Biological specificity driving the mode/mode-cluster results has been lost when generating a single brain-age delta.
source: This suggests that biological specificity driving the mode/mode-cluster results has been lost (diluted) when generating a single brain-age delta.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of genetic associations between individual modes and all-in-one models.

claim: 57 of the 62 modes were significantly heritable.
source: Finally, estimates of genetic (SNP) heritability showed that 57 of the 62 modes were significantly heritable, as were all 6 mode-clusters (see Materials and methods and online supplemental results).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the heritability analysis results.

claim: All 6 mode-clusters were significantly heritable.
source: Finally, estimates of genetic (SNP) heritability showed that 57 of the 62 modes were significantly heritable, as were all 6 mode-clusters (see Materials and methods and online supplemental results).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the heritability analysis results.

claim: None of the modes of aging map strongly onto Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease genetically after multiple comparison correction.
source: Estimates of co-heritability with Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease showed a small number of nominally significant results, but none of these survive multiple comparison correction across modes; this suggests that none of these modes of aging map strongly onto these diseases genetically.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the co-heritability analysis results and their interpretation.

claim: Associations were computed between all modes' deltas and 8787 non-imaging-derived phenotypes (nIDPs) spanning 16 groups of variable types.
source: We also computed associations between all modes' deltas and 8787 nIDPs (non-imaging-derived phenotypes), spanning 16 groups of variable types.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging association analysis methodology.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 is dominated by the volumes of the lateral ventricles and choroid plexus, the microstructure of the fornix and corpus callosum, and the volume of the thalamic nuclei.
source: Mode-cluster 16, which shows the strongest aging effect of the mode-clusters, is dominated by the volumes of the lateral ventricles and choroid plexus (and its intensity), the microstructure of the fornix and corpus callosum, and the volume of the thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 16, based on the IDP weights analysis.

claim: Fornix, choroid plexus and corpus callosum are all drained by the superior choroid vein.
source: Notably, and of relevance to further results discussed below, fornix, choroid plexus and corpus callosum are all drained by the superior choroid vein, which runs along the whole length of the choroid plexus, and unites with the superior thalamostriate vein, which itself drains the thalamic nuclei (and striatum).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical knowledge relevant to interpreting the mode composition.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 was associated with modifiable risk factors including heart rate, smoking, alcohol consumption and diabetes.
source: The non-imaging associations of mode-cluster 16 included many modifiable risk factors such as heart rate, smoking, alcohol consumption and diabetes, (as well as taking metformin, a treatment for diabetes, although this is likely an indirect association that is essentially an indicator of the presence of diabetes).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging associations found for mode-cluster 16.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 was associated with measures related to overall non-fat body size including height, strength, lung capacity, metabolic rate and weight.
source: It is also associated with various measures related to overall non-fat body size: height, strength, lung capacity, metabolic rate and weight, as well as multiple sclerosis.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging associations found for mode-cluster 16.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 was associated with multiple sclerosis.
source: It is also associated with various measures related to overall non-fat body size: height, strength, lung capacity, metabolic rate and weight, as well as multiple sclerosis.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the disease association found for mode-cluster 16.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 was associated with processing speed.
source: With regard to cognition, mode-cluster 16 was associated with processing speed.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the cognitive association found for mode-cluster 16.

claim: Mode-cluster 16 is associated with SNP rs4141741 (MED8), which was significantly correlated with blood pressure and diagnosed vascular and heart problems in UK Biobank participants.
source: Consistent with the contribution of the identified modifiable risk factors, mode-cluster 16 is associated with SNP rs4141741 (MED8), which was significantly correlated in the UK Biobank participants with blood pressure and diagnosed vascular and heart problems.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association and its phenotypic correlates.

claim: SNP rs4141741 is an eQTL in the hippocampus of TIE1, which codes for a protein playing a critical role in angiogenesis and blood vessel stability.
source: The same SNP is an eQTL in the hippocampus of TIE1, which codes for a protein playing a critical role in angiogenesis and blood vessel stability, and of MED8 in the striatum, both structures being innervated by the superior choroid and thalamostriate veins.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional annotation of the SNP, based on eQTL databases.

claim: Mode 1162 (ventricle volume) is associated with SNP 7:2777917_TA_T (rs1392800372), which is likely in gene GNA12.
source: Mode 1162 (ventricle volume) is associated with SNP 7:2777917_TA_T (rs1392800372), which is likely in gene GNA12; this has been found to relate to migration of neurons in the developing brain (Moers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with citation to functional evidence.

claim: GNA12 has been found to relate to migration of neurons in the developing brain.
source: Mode 1162 (ventricle volume) is associated with SNP 7:2777917_TA_T (rs1392800372), which is likely in gene GNA12; this has been found to relate to migration of neurons in the developing brain (Moers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about gene function supported by citation.

claim: Mode 262 (fornix MD) is associated with SNP rs150434736 near gene GMNC, which has been linked to Alzheimer's disease endophenotypes.
source: In line with mode-cluster 16 being dominated by the volumetric measure of CSF (cerebro-spinal fluid, which fills the ventricles), mode 262 (fornix MD) is associated with SNP rs150434736 (on chromosome 3, only 17kbp from the 3:190657741_AGT_A/rs147817028 peak in mode-cluster 16), near gene GMNC; this has been found to be linked to Alzheimer's disease endophenotypes (in particular ptau 181 in CSF) (Cruchaga et al., 2013; Deming et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with citations to functional evidence.

claim: Mode-cluster 26 relates to global measures of grey and white matter volume.
source: Mode-cluster 26 relates to global measures of grey and white matter volume.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 26.

claim: Mode-cluster 26 was associated with body-size-related non-imaging measures including height, weight, strength, metabolic rate and lung function.
source: It was associated with body-size-related non-imaging measures in common with mode-cluster 16, including those of height, weight, strength, metabolic rate and lung function, and also cognitive reaction time.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging associations found for mode-cluster 26.

claim: Mode-cluster 26 was associated with cognitive reaction time.
source: It was associated with body-size-related non-imaging measures in common with mode-cluster 16, including those of height, weight, strength, metabolic rate and lung function, and also cognitive reaction time.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the cognitive association found for mode-cluster 26.

claim: Mode 3262 (parietal/occipital volume) was associated with maternal smoking.
source: These modes did not have many nIDP associations (i.e. the nIDP associations for the mode-cluster were largely not regionally specific to individual modes), although mode 3262 (parietal/occipital volume) was associated with maternal smoking.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a specific non-imaging association.

claim: Modes 1662 and 1962 (hippocampus volume) were significantly associated with HRK, which is involved in apoptosis/neurogenesis, particularly in adults in hippocampus.
source: Modes 1662 and 1962 (hippocampus volume) were found to be significantly associated with HRK; this is involved in apoptosis/neurogenesis, particularly in adults in hippocampus (Coultas et al., 2007), and expressed (eQTL) in hippocampus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with citation to functional evidence.

claim: Mode 4062 (volume of the precuneus cortical region) was associated with DAAM1, important for cell polarity and neural development.
source: Mode 4062 (volume of the precuneus cortical region) was associated with DAAM1 (Elliott, 2018; Mollink et al., 2019), important for cell polarity and neural development.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with citations.

claim: Mode 162 is associated with smoking and alcohol.
source: While the above modes relate to regionally-specific grey matter volume, there is also involvement (in this mode-cluster) of mode 162; this codes for total grey matter volume and is the most strongly age-related mode. This mode is associated with smoking and alcohol, as well as bone density (as measured separately from the MRI, using DEXA low-dose x-ray and also ultrasound).
evidence: This is a direct statement of non-imaging associations for mode 162.

claim: The greater bone density loss in females is likely to be associated with menopause.
source: The greater bone density loss in females is likely to be associated with menopause.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sex-specific pattern and association with age-at-menopause.

claim: Mode 162 is significantly associated with age-at-menopause.
source: Firstly, this mode is significantly associated with age-at-menopause (a non-imaging variable in UK Biobank, with average age-at-menopause being 50y).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a non-imaging association.

claim: Bone density loss is specifically accelerated in the 10 years after menopause.
source: More generally, there is a large amount of literature showing that bone density loss is specifically accelerated in the 10 years after menopause (O'Flaherty, 2000); this exactly matches the sex-specific pattern of change in females seen in this mode (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to literature and visual evidence in Figure 5.

claim: Mode 162 shows an increase in T1-weighted intensity within the skull, reflecting an increase in bone marrow fat with increasing brain-age delta.
source: Figure 5A, B shows the increase in T1-weighted intensity within the skull, associated with this mode. This is reflecting an increase in bone marrow fat with increasing brain-age delta.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an imaging observation with interpretation, supported by Figure 5.

claim: The increase in bone marrow fat with brain-age delta is consistent with literature regarding decreasing bone density and increasing marrow in aging.
source: This, together with the above nIDP associations with bone density loss in this mode, is consistent with literature regarding decreasing bone density and increasing marrow in aging (Cordes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement connecting the findings to existing literature via citation.

claim: Bone density reduction has been linked to early Alzheimer's disease, independent of age, sex, habitual physical activity, smoking, depression and estrogen replacement status.
source: Bone density reduction has not just been reported in normal aging, but has also been linked to early Alzheimer's disease, independent of age, sex, habitual physical activity, smoking, depression and estrogen replacement status (Loskutova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Mode 162 has one strong genetic association with lead SNP rs3801383, whose PHEWAS results are dominated by bone density associations.
source: These results are consistent with the one strong genetic association with mode 162 (Figure 5E); lead SNP rs3801383 (whose PHEWAS results are dominated by bone density associations - see Materials and methods) lies within the span of FAM3C, but also is in LD with SNPs spanning across to genes WNT16 and CPED1 (Chesi et al., 2015; Movérare-Skrtic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with supporting evidence from PHEWAS and citations.

claim: FAM3C is associated with bone density loss and bone fractures in UK Biobank genetic data.
source: FAM3C is associated (in UK Biobank genetic data http://big.stats.ox.ac.uk) with bone density loss and bone fractures, but has also been linked directly to Alzheimer's disease through impact on brain amyloid (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of genetic associations found in UK Biobank data and literature, supported by citation.

claim: FAM3C has been linked directly to Alzheimer's disease through impact on brain amyloid.
source: FAM3C is associated (in UK Biobank genetic data http://big.stats.ox.ac.uk) with bone density loss and bone fractures, but has also been linked directly to Alzheimer's disease through impact on brain amyloid (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Mode-cluster 36 represents T1-weighted intensity contrast between white and grey matter across the grey-white border.
source: Mode-cluster 36 singles out IDPs representing T1-weighted intensity contrast between white and grey matter (across the grey-white border).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 36.

claim: Mode-cluster 36 mainly relates to measures of fat mass and fat percentages across the body, as well as blood haemoglobin measures.
source: Although mode-clusters 16 and 26 related to weight, they were essentially driven by non-fat mass; here, however, mode-cluster 36 mainly relates to measures of fat mass and fat percentages across the body, as well as blood haemoglobin measures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging associations found for mode-cluster 36.

claim: Mode-cluster 36 is associated with SNP rs12133923, an eQTL of CREB3L4 in the basal ganglia, which regulates adipogenesis.
source: In line with these non-imaging correlations, one strong genetic association was found for a SNP (rs12133923), an eQTL of CREB3L4 in the basal ganglia and of CRTC2, SLC27A3 and S100A16 in the cerebellum. CREB3L4, which regulates adipogenesis, has for instance been recently shown to have a critical role in metabolic phenotypes (weight gain, impaired glucose tolerance and decreased insulin sensitivity) (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with functional annotation and citation.

claim: The marked, widespread change of cortical contrast with aging is strongly related to the fatty, lipid-rich myelin.
source: Taken altogether, it is therefore likely that the marked, widespread change of cortical contrast with aging witnessed here (and in several previous studies) is strongly related to the fatty, lipid-rich myelin (Salat et al., 2009; Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of associations, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mode-cluster 36 was associated with SNP rs1044595 in an exon of STX6, in high LD with a SNP associated with tauopathy progressive supranuclear palsy.
source: Of note, mode-cluster 36 was also strongly associated with other SNPs, amongst them one (rs1044595) in an exon of STX6, and in high LD with a SNP associated with tauopathy progressive supranuclear palsy (Höglinger et al., 2011), and correlated in the UK Biobank participants with hormonal replacement treatment.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with citation and phenotypic correlates.

claim: Mode-cluster 46 is strongly linked to modifiable risk factors including high blood pressure, vascular and heart problems.
source: Mode-cluster 46 is strongly linked to modifiable risk factors: high blood pressure, vascular and heart problems, and associated with taking ramipril (a treatment against high blood pressure and heart failure).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-imaging associations found for mode-cluster 46.

claim: Mode-cluster 46 is characterised by diffusion measures of mostly frontal white matter.
source: Mode-cluster 46 is characterised by diffusion measures of mostly frontal white matter (anterior corona radiata and, overlapping in the frontal lobe, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), and was also associated with general reaction time.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 46.

claim: Mode-cluster 46 was associated with general reaction time.
source: Mode-cluster 46 is characterised by diffusion measures of mostly frontal white matter (anterior corona radiata and, overlapping in the frontal lobe, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), and was also associated with general reaction time.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a cognitive association.

claim: Mode-cluster 46 subject-weights have very little age dependence after partialling out other mode-clusters.
source: The subject-weights are strongly age-dependent (as are all mode-clusters); however, they have very little age dependence after partialling out other mode-clusters; this means that the above factors interact in a manner that is largely age-independent.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an analytical finding about the unique variance of mode-cluster 46.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 shows a modest deceleration of aging-rate with increasing age, particularly with respect to its unique variance.
source: Mode-cluster 56 shows a modest deceleration of aging-rate with increasing age, particularly with respect to its unique (partialled) variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a direct statement of an analytical finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 involves just the amplitudes of resting-state fluctuations, covering most of the brain.
source: It involves just the amplitudes of resting-state fluctuations, covering most of the brain; some of the associated modes also show rfMRI connection-strength involvement, but that may be an indirect result of the amplitude changes.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 56.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 demonstrated strong correlations with weight, fat mass and percentage, red blood cell count and haemoglobin.
source: Mode-cluster 56 demonstrated strong correlations with non-imaging variables similar to mode-cluster 36: weight, fat mass and percentage, red blood cell count and haemoglobin.
evidence: This is a direct statement of non-imaging associations.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 was associated with blood pressure, cardiac output and bone density, along with sleep duration, nervous feelings and several markers of socio-economic status.
source: It also was associated with blood pressure, cardiac output and bone density, along with sleep duration, nervous feelings and several markers of socio-economic status (SES).
evidence: This is a direct statement of non-imaging associations.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 was strongly associated with SNP rs4497325, and for the associated mode 4562, the peak SNP is rs7096828, an eQTL of INPP5A, which is involved in DNA methylation in neurons, associated with aging and depression.
source: The strongest GWAS hit is rs4497325, and for the associated mode 4562, the peak SNP is (the immediately-neighbouring) rs7096828; this is an eQTL of INPP5A, which is involved in DNA methylation in neurons, associated with aging and depression (Gasparoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with functional annotation and citation.

claim: Mode-cluster 56 has a genetic association with rs429358, the SNP that determines whether the APOE allele is ε4 or not.
source: Finally, a genetic association was found with rs429358, the SNP that determines whether the APOE allele is ε4 or not.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association.

claim: rs429358 is a major locus associated with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
source: This is a major locus associated with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment, and also with dementia with Lewy bodies, age at onset of symptoms in Parkinson's disease, insomnia, brain amyloid deposition and neurofibrillary tangles, inflammation, HDL/LDL cholesterol and triglycerides levels, physical activity and blood protein levels, parental longevity, and macular degeneration.
evidence: This is a statement of known associations for this SNP, based on established knowledge.

claim: Despite being associated with SES, mental health markers, and functional MRI amplitude fluctuations, mode-cluster 56 had no direct associations with cognitive test scores.
source: Despite being associated with SES, mental health markers, functional MRI amplitude fluctuations, and SNPs involved in cognitive decline, there were no direct associations between this mode-cluster (or its associated modes) and cognitive test scores.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the absence of certain associations.

claim: Mode 4162 links amplitude of rfMRI fluctuations in visual cortex to age when started using glasses.
source: The link between SES and fMRI activity levels seen in Figure 7C in Miller et al. (2016) may now be explained; here, mode 4162 links amplitude of rfMRI fluctuations in visual cortex to age when started using glasses (and indeed we looked at age subgroups to confirm that this association is driven by those subjects who started wearing glasses while younger than 30y).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a specific association with additional validation.

claim: Mode-cluster 66 was entirely composed of grey matter thickness IDPs, mainly in the prefrontal areas, as well as higher order parietal and temporal regions.
source: Mode-cluster66 was entirely composed of grey matter thickness IDPs, mainly in the prefrontal areas, as well as higher order parietal and temporal regions.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging features associated with mode-cluster 66.

claim: Mode-cluster 66 correlated with non-imaging variables of weight, red blood cells and head bone density.
source: It correlated with non-imaging variables of weight, red blood cells and head bone density.
evidence: This is a direct statement of non-imaging associations.

claim: Mode-cluster 66 was age-dependent, but its unique variance was only weakly so.
source: This mode-cluster was age-dependent, but its unique (partialled) variance was only weakly so.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an analytical finding about the unique variance.

claim: Mode-cluster 66 has a genetic association with rs682571 in an intron of MACF1, which regulates the migration of pyramidal neurons and cortical GABAergic interneurons.
source: We found three genetic associations with Cluster 6. The first, rs682571, is in an intron of MACF1, which has been shown recently to regulate the migration of pyramidal neurons and cortical GABAergic interneurons (Ka et al., 2014; Ka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with functional annotation and citations.

claim: Mode-cluster 66 has a genetic association with rs13107325 in an exon of SLC39A8 (ZIP8), which has been found in GWAS studies looking at medication use, tobacco and alcohol consumption, cholesterol, body fat, adiposity, osteoarthritis, red blood cell, blood pressure, sleep duration, risk taking, intelligence/math ability/cognitive function and schizophrenia.
source: Another hit, rs13107325, is in an exon (missense) of SLC39A8 (ZIP8), the same SNP reported in our GWAS-IDP study (Elliott, 2018) to be associated with subcortical and cerebellar volume and susceptibility. This has also been found in other GWAS studies (many based primarily on UK Biobank data), including those looking at medication use, tobacco and alcohol consumption, cholesterol, body fat, adiposity, osteoarthritis, red blood cell, blood pressure, sleep duration, risk taking, intelligence/math ability/cognitive function and schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a genetic association with extensive phenotypic correlates from previous studies.

claim: 17 modes and three mode-clusters show statistically significant amount of non-additive brain aging.
source: The results are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10. 17 modes and three mode-clusters show statistically significant amount of non-additive brain aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the non-additive modeling results with reference to a figure.

claim: In most cases of non-additive brain aging, delta is either constant or increases with aging.
source: In most cases (e.g. C, mode 462), delta is either constant or increases with aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the pattern observed in non-additive modeling with reference to a figure example.

claim: In a few cases of non-additive brain aging, delta is decreasing with age.
source: In a few cases (e.g. D, mode 1162), delta is decreasing with age.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a pattern observed in non-additive modeling with reference to a figure example.

claim: Mode 5362 involves changes in white matter fibre organisation in the posterior thalamic radiation and was associated with glaucoma.
source: Mode 5362 involves changes in white matter fibre organisation in the posterior thalamic radiation (also known as the optic radiation, and connecting to visual cortex), and was associated with glaucoma, as previously reported (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement of imaging features and disease association with citation.

claim: Mode 5062 involves changes in white matter diffusivity in the superior cerebellar peduncle and was associated with IQ and several markers of socio-economic status.
source: Mode 5062 involves changes in white matter diffusivity in the superior cerebellar peduncle, and was associated with IQ and several markers of socio-economic status.
evidence: This is a direct statement of imaging features and non-imaging associations.

claim: Modes with unique variance contributing to reducing brain age may represent cognitive reserve.
source: In such cases, where a mode's unique variance is contributing to reducing (and not increasing) brain age, one possible interpretation is that the mode represents cognitive reserve, that is, working against the general pattern of age-related decline (indeed, aspects of socio-economic status are frequently used as proxies for cognitive reserve).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on established concepts in the field.
